issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette: As a renowned film director, Thomas had always been drawn to the thrill of capturing life's most intense moments on camera. But it was during a shoot in an abandoned warehouse that his own life took a drastic turn. A sudden collapse of the structure left him trapped under the rubble, fighting for air and consciousness. The memories of those harrowing minutes are forever seared into his mind like vivid frames of a film he can't shake. In the aftermath, Thomas began to question his own adequacy as a director and, more fundamentally, as a person. He couldn't help but wonder why this had happened to him - was it some cosmic punishment for pushing the limits too far? These ruminations on inadequacy soon spilled over into other areas of his life. He started feeling like he was losing himself, becoming someone unrecognizable even to those closest to him, including his partner. As these negative self-appraisals took hold, Thomas found himself employing various maladaptive strategies to cope with the anxiety that now gripped him. He avoided dark places or enclosed spaces, instinctively associating them with the suffocating sensation he experienced during the accident. He also became a master of distraction, filling every spare moment with work or meaningless activities to avoid confronting his thoughts and memories. But these avoidance tactics only seemed to heighten Thomas's sense of threat. The world began to feel like a minefield of potential dangers - loud noises made him jump, and he found himself perpetually on edge, scanning for signs of impending doom. Even the creaks and groans of the old film sets where he worked now sent his heart racing. Memories of that fateful day lingered, refusing to be silenced. Thomas would see flashes of debris falling, hear the sound of crumbling concrete - it was as if the event had become an indelible part of him. He struggled to verbalize these memories; they remained stubbornly nonverbal, manifesting instead in a perpetual sense of unease that colored every waking moment. These fragmented recollections not only contributed to his threat appraisal but also reinforced Thomas's negative self-perceptions. Why couldn't he shake off the feeling of being an inadequate person? The accident had happened on his watch; it was a stark reminder that, no matter how much control he exerted over his film sets, life itself remained unpredictably cruel. In turn, these intensified feelings of inadequacy led Thomas to rely even more heavily on maladaptive strategies - more distraction, more avoidance. It became a self-reinforcing cycle where his inability to confront the past fed into an ever-present sense of danger, which in turn drove him further away from confronting those very memories. Despite this vicious loop, it was only when Thomas found himself at odds with his long-time partner over his increasing withdrawal that he realized he needed help. The fear of losing not just himself but also the people he loved most finally brought him to seek therapy - a move he hoped would be the first step towards reclaiming his life and breaking free from the suffocating grip of his memories.
